what_it_does: Hardware security researchers want to attach small labels (metadata tags) to every instruction in a program so the processor can enforce rules like 'never jump to an address that wasn't declared as a valid function entry point' — a defense against attacks that hijack program control flow. Adding these tags today requires custom, architecture-specific hacks to the compiler (the tool that translates source code into machine instructions), making the approach laborious to deploy and hard to reuse across different tag policies. COGENT is a toolchain built on top of LLVM (a widely used open-source compiler infrastructure) that automatically adds variable-width tags — anywhere from 1 to 32 bits per instruction, or wider tags per function or code block — to RISC-V binaries (RISC-V is an open-source chip instruction set). A special compiler pass marks branch targets and function call sites to support control-flow integrity (CFI — the policy that prevents a program from being redirected to arbitrary code), and the toolchain is designed so new tag policies can be added without touching the compiler core.
